title: Who I am
job: Introduce yourself and state what you like

rules.text: Subject–Verb–Object order works, just like English.
"To be" vanishes in the present: ismī Rohān ("my-name Rohan") — no is/am.
The subject usually lives inside the verb: uḥibb = I-like, urīd = I-want.
General statements keep the article: English "I like coffee" → Arabic "I like THE coffee" (al-qahwa).

words.note: ism (name) + the attached -ī = "my". Possession is a suffix, not a word.

sentences.trap: No "is" — Arabic drops the verb "to be" in the present. "ismī huwa Rohān" sounds stilted.
sentences.sound: Say it ISS-mee ro-HAAN — crisp double s, long final vowels.

variations.changed: -ī (my) → -hu (his) — the owner hangs off the end

mistake.why: The present-tense "to be" (huwa) is dropped — ismī Rohān is complete.

sentences.mnemonic: ismī = "name-my" — the owner hangs off the end of the word.

words.note: Pronoun "I" — needed here because there is no verb. The same slot takes anta / anti (you) or huwa (he).
Country names usually take al- ("the India").

sentences.trap: English says "from India"; Arabic keeps the article — min al-Hind, not min Hind.
sentences.sound: Run it together: a-NAA min al-HIND.

variations.changed: anā → anta: the pronoun carries the person, since there is no verb
anā → huwa — same frame, third person, still no verb

mistake.why: No "am" to translate — anā min al-Hind is already the whole sentence.

sentences.usage: Where you are from — the second or third line of any introduction.
sentences.mnemonic: al-Hind carries its own "the" — Arabic says "the India".

words.note: One verb covers like and love; the subject "I" lives inside the verb.
General statements take al- — English drops "the", Arabic keeps it.

sentences.trap: "uḥibb qahwa" (no al-) sounds like "I like a coffee". Liking coffee in general needs al-qahwa.
sentences.sound: The q of qahwa is a deep k from the back of the throat — u-HIBB al-QAH-wa.

variations.changed: u- → tu-: the person prefix swaps, al-qahwa stays
swap the thing liked — al- rides along with it

mistake.why: Drop the extra anā (it is already inside the verb) and keep al-: uḥibb al-qahwa.

sentences.usage: Likes of every kind — food, people, places.
sentences.mnemonic: ḥubb = love — Arabic "likes" by loving; the same root as ḥabībī.

words.note: The everyday wanting verb; "I" is inside it.
The ʾ is a tiny catch in the throat. Plain māʾ is water in general; al-māʾ is that particular water.

sentences.trap: Asking for something is the one place al- drops off: urīd māʾ, not urīd al-māʾ — the opposite of uḥibb al-qahwa.
sentences.sound: u-REED māʾ — end on the little throat-catch, not a long aah.

variations.changed: u- → tu-: the wanting is now yours
add al- — that water on the table, not water in general

mistake.why: Drop the anā — the "I" is already inside urīd.

sentences.usage: Asking for what you want — shops, tables, homes.
sentences.mnemonic: urīd sounds like "you read" — but it is I-want; the u- at the front is the "I".
